newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FEATURE - Slovakia's dambuilder lambasts his critics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Slovakia's dambuilder lambasts his critics.

text.p: Julius Binder has the confidence of a man who has achieved his life's ambition -- to harness Europe's mighty Danube -- despite all the efforts of ministers and environmentalists to stop him.

Seated in his office looking overlooking his project, the vast Gabcikovo hydroelectric power station, the man who defied even his own government by diverting the great river to feed his creation has an uncompromising view of his work.

"Nature has to be protected by man but nature also has to serve man," he told Reuters in firm but soft tones. "If you read the Bible at the very beginning you can find nature was given to men to protect but also to exploit."

Binder's determination to see through what has been described as Europe's last great Stalinist project has been undimmed since he became general director 12 years ago of Vodohospodarska Vystavba, the company entrusted with the task of building the Gabcikovo dam.

The barrage, situated 50 km (30 miles) east of the Slovak capital Bratislava and which satisfies 12 percent of Slovakia's energy needs, was originally part of a 1977 plan agreed by the then Communist governments of Czechoslovakia and Hungary
It is also currently the subject of a bitter dispute being fought out between Hungary and Slovakia at the U.N. International Court of Justice.
This week, the Hague judges will visit the region to see the project and its consequences for themselves -- the first time the court has ever left its headquarters .

Hungary, with whom Slovakia shares the Danube as a common border, suspended work on a companion dam downstream at Nagymaros in 1989 after pressure from environmental groups, and in 1992 it pulled out of the project altogether.
CRITICS ACKNOWLEDGE "IMPRESSIVE TECHNICAL FEAT"

While talks between the Hungarian and the then Czechoslovak governments dragged on, Binder's company was preparing a huge 25 km-long, 300-metre (900 foot) wide channel to feed the Danube waters into the massive Gabcikovo turbines.
The diversion was part of a plan -- called Variant C -- to make the project feasible without the technical help of Hungary. The preparations took just 11 months.

"It has to be said it was an impressive technical feat," said Alexander Zinke of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), who has repeatedly expressed the WWF's concerns over the environmental effect of the project.
"German engineers I talked to said it would take five years to do what they did," he said. "I'm afraid the Hungarians made the mistake of underestimating what the Slovaks could do."

Such thoughts were a red flag to Binder, whose zeal to complete the project is bound up with his patriotic dedication to Slovak independence after centuries of Hungarian, Austrian and, most recently, Czech rule.
"We proved when we proceeded with Variant C that Slovaks are capable of building a big project and this was one of the examples of how we deserved to have our own state," he said.
In October 1992, when the European Union urged temporary suspension of building work, Binder was getting nervous.
"As an engineer he knew that if he didn't divert the water within days in the early winter's dry season he'd have to wait another year before the river would be low enough," said Zinke.
On Saturday, October 24, while the Slovak government was still considering its next move, hundreds of trucks began dumping huge boulders into the Danube.
VILLAGERS COMPLAIN OF SUBSIDING FOUNDATIONS
Within days 80 percent of the river had been diverted into the new channel, whose embankments tower up to 18 metres (60 feet) above the Slovak plain, dwarfing the villages beneath it.

"It was like the eighth wonder of the world," remembers Imre Boosi, mayor of the Hungarian village of Asvanyraro. "The huge river we'd known all our lives suddenly became just a trickle at the bottom of a massive dry river bed."
For Asvanyraro's 2,000 residents the effect was devastating. By 1994, 212 of the 700 households in the village had reported cracks in their walls, while 289 said their wells had dried up.

Following a meeting between Slovak and Hungarian Prime ministers Gyula Horn and Vladimir Meciar, Slovakia agreed to increase the water it diverted into the old river bed to an average 400 cubic metres per second from around 200, but still only a fifth of the original flow.
In order to maximise the effect of the increased water, Binder built a series of dykes across the wetlands either side of the old river bed to hold back water where necessary.
Consequently, the Hague judges will see plenty of water but Zinke says they will be looking at a fundamentally changed ecosystem.

"There's plenty of greenery and birdsong but instead of periodic flooding which serves to swill out the side channels and enable pioneer species to move in and out, we now have a pond system with fewer species of both plant and animal life."
Binder claims his dykes have improved the environment, notably upriver near Bratislava where the water table has been raised.
But he says the whole environmental debate is a distraction from a much bigger issue related to Hungary's historical ascendancy over Slovakia, which used to be part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

"(The environment) is just a fog around the problem and the problem is the border," he said. "Let's be open. Hungary still considers Slovakia the northern part of their country. The 1977 treaty was a problem because it recognised current borders."

Such allegations are vehemently denied by the Hungarian government, who point to the recent treaty between Hungary and Slovakia, which forbids the alteration of current borders, as evidence that Budapest has no designs on Slovakia.
However, such arguments cloud an already complicated environmental issue which the Hague court will not be in a position to resolve.

Its brief is only to decide whether Hungary had the right to renege on the 1977 treaty and whether Slovakia was right to divert the Danube. The betting is on a "no' on both counts, leaving the two sides no nearer agreement on what to do with Julius Binder's dream fulfilled.
